team.summary: Three co-founders, all former Apple engineers who built core depth-sensing and perception technology for Face ID. Strong founder-market fit for robotics perception; deep technical expertise in computer vision and sensor fusion. No prior startup exits or operating experience disclosed.

founders.name: Alexander Shpunt
founders.background: Ex-Apple engineer; contributed to Face ID depth-sensing and perception technology.

product.plainLanguage: Robotics perception and environment understanding stack — software and algorithms that let robots see, interpret, and navigate the physical world.
product.category: Robotics perception / Computer vision for robotics

market.competitiveLandscape: Competes with established sensor/perception platforms (e.g., NVIDIA Isaac, Intel RealSense, specialized startups like Slamcore, Zivid) and in-house robotics stacks.
market.whyNow: Convergence of cheaper depth sensors, matured deep learning for 3D vision, and surging demand for autonomous mobile robots in logistics/manufacturing; founders bring proprietary Face ID‑grade perception IP.

risks.text: No prior startup founding or exit experience among the team; execution risk in transitioning from big‑tech R&D to a standalone product company.
Defensibility unclear: no disclosed proprietary data moat, workflow lock‑in, or network effects; differentiation may rely solely on algorithmic superiority which can be eroded.
Product is a perception component, not an end‑to‑end AI agent; go‑to‑market likely requires deep integration with robot OEMs, not self‑serve SMB onboarding.
Market size and traction unproven: $107M funding at launch signals investor confidence but no paying customers, active usage, or product launch disclosed yet.

subScores.label: Team
subScores.rationale: Exceptional founder-market fit and technical depth (Apple Face ID perception leads); however, zero prior startup/exit experience tempers the score.

subScores.label: Defensibility
subScores.rationale: Strong proprietary algorithmic IP from Face ID work, but no evidence of data moat, workflow lock-in, or network effects; differentiation currently rests on technical lead which may not be durable.

subScores.label: Product
subScores.rationale: Clear one-sentence description, but it is a perception library/component — not an AI-native agent that acts end-to-end, and not self-serve for SMBs (targets robot OEMs with heavy integration).

subScores.label: Market & Why-Now
subScores.rationale: Credible vertical (robotics perception) with plausible why-now (sensor cost drops, AI maturity, autonomy demand), but no size hint or articulated wedge beyond founder pedigree.

subScores.label: Traction / Freshness
subScores.rationale: Very fresh, high-signal event: $107M raise at launch (Jan 2026). No paying customers or usage data yet, so signal is purely financial and recent.

scoreRationale: Lyte AI scores highly on team and fresh funding traction, but product and defensibility are early-stage risks. The perception stack is a component play in a crowded, capital-intensive market; without demonstrated workflow lock-in or a self-serve wedge, the investment thesis hinges on the team converting Apple-grade IP into a defensible, scalable robotics platform.
